title: Monotonicity and competitive equilibrium in cake-cutting
summary_en: Cake-cutting — fairly dividing a divisible good among agents — is the canonical fair-division problem. Segal-Halevi and Sziklai study competitive equilibria in cake-cutting markets and ask when a small change in agents' preferences leads to a smooth (monotone) change in the equilibrium allocation. They identify the preference and divisibility conditions under which equilibrium is monotone, and exhibit examples where small preference perturbations cause discontinuous reallocations.
data_used: Theoretical paper. No primary dataset; results are formal characterisations of equilibrium properties in cake-cutting markets.
policy_relevance: Theoretical foundation for fair-division mechanisms used in inheritance and divorce settlements, EU regional-budget allocation, and equitable-distribution rules in privatisation episodes. Practical takeaway for any policy that cuts an indivisible-but-shareable resource (broadcast spectrum, EU agricultural quotas): monotonicity of the allocation rule matters for predictability when underlying valuations shift.
